text:
Education in Finland is characterized by a comprehensive, equitable, and student-centered system. Compulsory education spans from age 7 to 18, including a nine-year comprehensive school (peruskoulu) and mandatory upper secondary education (lukio or ammattikoulu). Early childhood education is universally accessible and emphasizes play-based learning, social development, and reading for pleasure, with free daycare available from age 8 months to 5 years. The system is highly decentralized, with schools funded and administered by municipalities, and teachers are fully unionized, enjoying significant autonomy in pedagogy and curriculum. Small class sizes (typically under 20 students) and minimal homework foster a relaxed, supportive learning environment.
Grading is primarily qualitative, with verbal assessments and a 4–10 scale, and students may repeat a year only if they fail multiple subjects. There are no high-stakes standardized tests. Upper secondary education offers both academic and vocational tracks, with vocational graduates gaining access to university of applied sciences. Tertiary education includes traditional universities (focused on research and theory) and universities of applied sciences (focused on practical, work-related training). Admissions are merit-based, transparent, and objective, with no essays or human bias. Tuition is free for EU/EEA students, though non-EU students pay fees since 2017.
The system emphasizes lifelong learning, with strong support for adult education through free institutions and open university programs. Finland's education model is globally recognized for its success, and it is currently undergoing reforms to integrate phenomenon-based learning (phenomenon-based learning) into the curriculum, promoting 21st-century skills such as critical thinking and collaboration. The country also exports its educational philosophy through international schools and programs, maintaining a strong focus on equity, well-being, and holistic development.
